summary: This document describes Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR), a mechanism to minimize packet loss when a fault hits the IP network carrying multicast services such as IPTV. It is informational and describes a technique rather than a standard.

eli5.summary: Imagine getting the same TV show sent along two roads. If one road is blocked, you just keep watching from the other with no gap. That is the idea here.

questions: how to reduce iptv packet loss
how does mofrr protect multicast streams
subtitle: Multicast protection using dual paths to handle network failures fast.

tldr.problem: Multicast services like IPTV need fast recovery when the network path fails, but waiting for the routing protocols to detect and repair the failure causes packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: MoFRR pre-builds a second path to the multicast source and receives data on both paths simultaneously. It accepts packets only from the primary path and discards the secondary ones. When the primary fails, it switches to the secondary path within milliseconds.
tldr.outcome: Packet loss during failures drops from seconds to tens of milliseconds, making IPTV and other multicast services more reliable without needing protocol changes.

facts.label: Suitable topologies
facts.value: Dual-plane networks, data centers with meshed layers

today: RFC 7431 is an Informational RFC describing a proven technique used in production multicast networks. It has not been obsoleted and remains a relevant approach for protecting multicast services in properly designed topologies.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Multicast services such as IPTV need to broadcast video to thousands of viewers at once. When a network link or router on the path from the source to a viewer fails, the whole stream stops for that viewer until the network re-learns the topology and establishes a new tree. This reconvergence can take several seconds, causing visible outages.

Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) solves this by making a single change to how multicast routing works: instead of using just one path to the source, a merge point (the router closest to the viewers) joins the tree using two different paths at the same time. Data flows over both paths, but only the primary is used. When the primary fails, the router instantly switches to the secondary, which is already active and carrying traffic.
sections.eli5: The router gets data from two different upstream directions and only uses one. If that one breaks, it instantly switches to the other without waiting for routes to change.

sections.title: How Dual Paths Work
sections.content:
MoFRR requires no changes to the PIM or mLDP protocols themselves. Instead, it adds logic at merge point routers to determine two upstream multicast hops (UMHs): a primary and a secondary. Both are chosen using standard unicast routing rules to avoid loops.

The primary UMH is selected the same way it would be without MoFRR. The secondary is chosen using Loop-Free Alternates (LFA), which are alternate next-hops guaranteed not to cause routing loops. The two UMHs should be as diverse as possible—ideally, they reach the source via completely different paths.

A merge point receives complete multicast streams on both paths. It accepts packets from the primary and discards duplicates from the secondary. This is similar to how multicast already handles receiving the same stream on multiple interfaces.
sections.eli5: The router picks two different upstream neighbors as backups. One is the main choice, and one is the backup. Both send the stream, but only the main one is used until it fails.

sections.title: Detecting and Switching from Failure
sections.content:
MoFRR offers several ways to detect when the primary path has failed and trigger a switch to the secondary. The simplest is detecting the loss of the local interface, which can happen in about 50 milliseconds using BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection).

A second option compares the timestamp or sequence number of packets arriving on both paths and forwards whichever arrives first. For RTP-based streams (which carry timestamps), this can achieve zero packet loss because the stream has a steady packet rate.

A third option assumes a minimum known packet rate for the stream. If no packet arrives on the primary interface for longer than expected, the router assumes failure and switches to the secondary. This works well for high-rate services like IPTV, where packets arrive every few milliseconds.

Finally, when the IGP (interior gateway protocol, such as OSPF or IS-IS) withdraws the route to the primary UMH, the merge point switches to the secondary. This takes advantage of improvements in IGP convergence speed and ensures sub-second switchover in many cases.
sections.eli5: The router notices the main path is broken in one of several ways—a dead interface, no packets arriving, or the router no longer reachable. When it detects the break, it switches to the backup path instantly.

sections.title: When MoFRR Works Best
sections.content:
MoFRR is most effective in dual-plane network topologies, which are common in service provider networks. In a dual-plane design, routers have two disjoint paths to the source via two separate network planes. Each Provider Edge (PE) router can be dual-homed to one plane, with disjoint paths available through both planes. When MoFRR is enabled, each PE joins the primary path on its plane and a secondary path to a neighbor on the other plane, maximizing redundancy.

MoFRR can also apply to networks without strict dual planes. For example, pairs of PE routers can be connected to opposite planes, and each can use the peer's plane as a secondary path. However, capacity planning tools may be needed to verify that sufficient disjointness exists for acceptable protection coverage.

In arbitrary network topologies without planning, the secondary path might fail for the same reason as the primary, offering no protection. Therefore, MoFRR is most suitable for networks where topology design or capacity planning ensures that the primary and secondary paths remain diverse.
sections.eli5: This works great in networks designed with two separate paths everywhere. It can work in other shapes too, but network planners need to check that the backup path doesn't share the same weak spot as the main one.

sections.title: Deployment and Broader Applications
sections.content:
MoFRR is simple to deploy because it requires no PIM or mLDP protocol modifications. PE routers can be enabled one at a time, and there is no need for network-wide coordination or interoperability testing. Many service providers already have the disjoint paths required by MoFRR built into their network design.

Beyond IPTV and video on demand, MoFRR can benefit data centers where there is dense meshed connectivity between access, distribution, and core layers. A three-level hierarchy with inexpensive bandwidth connecting the layers offers natural ECMP paths at multiple layers, enabling redundancy protection at each layer with minimal overhead.

Because only the primary path forwards data, management tools like ping and mtrace will not verify the secondary path. MoFRR can also be applied to Multicast Virtual Private Networks (MVPNs).

The key advantage across all applications is that redundancy is achieved with minimal extra traffic. Secondary paths graft onto existing multicast trees at aggregation points and do not demand additional bandwidth on distribution or backbone links.
sections.eli5: Network operators just turn it on. It doesn't break anything else and uses bandwidth efficiently since both paths share trees where possible.
